To Gerhard Günther, in reply to his question about demonological literature:
Several times in my life I have gone on a similar search and eventually become stuck.
Baader contains several striking passages, but it is impossible to push much further.
Perhaps that lies in the nature of the subject.
The literature of lower magic is barren and repellent.
What interests me far more is the hidden demonic force inside concepts from intellectual history that, on the surface, appear perfectly respectable in the salon and the lecture hall.
Above all: the concept of genius. Here the connection with the events of 1925–45 is immediately obvious.
Beyond that, all I can say is that, so far as I know, René Guénon is today the best-informed author on the subject.
On the katechon: I believe in the katechon, the restraining power.
For me, it is the only way to understand history as a Christian and to find meaning in it.
Paul’s secret teaching is no more secret—and no less secret—than Christian existence itself.
Anyone who does not himself know, in concrete experience, something of the katechon cannot interpret the passage.
To Adso one must add Haimo of Halberstadt (Migne X.117, col. 779), who is Adso’s source and much clearer than Adso himself.
Today’s theologians no longer know this.
At bottom, they do not even want to know it.
What I really wanted to ask you was: Who is the katechon today?
Surely one cannot regard Churchill or John Foster Dulles as the katechon.
The question is more important than the question of Jünger’s Chief Forester.
For every age of the past 1,948 years, one must be able to name the katechon.
The position has never been vacant.
Otherwise we would no longer exist.

Every great emperor of the Christian Middle Ages believed, with complete faith and conscious certainty, that he was the katechon. And he was. It is simply impossible to write the history of the Middle Ages without seeing and understanding this central fact. There are temporary holders of this task.
I am sure that we could even agree on many concrete names right down to the present day, once the concept itself became clear enough.
Donoso Cortés failed theologically because this concept remained unknown to him.
Delusion everywhere. That is almost harmless compared with: deception everywhere!

Once every other deceiver has been discovered, and a human being finds himself alone, thrown back entirely upon himself, the stage of the worst deception begins: self-deception. That is where the age opened by Descartes now finds itself. It was a spiritus malignus, an evil spirit, whose bottomless deception Descartes regarded as possible. He shuddered before that possibility. He escaped from it through his cogito.
Today it is this self of ours that makes us shudder.
Foreign sound waves rush unheard through my space.
The fact that I do not hear them does not make my situation in space any better. It is as though invisible bullets were being fired all around me without hitting me.
Can I say here: what I do not know cannot hurt me?
Unfortunately, I do know it. There is consciousness of it.
I am no longer in the position of the Roman dominus and pater familias, lord and father of the household.
Are we simply supposed to throw off this awareness that our space is filled with alien things?
Leap back into the happiness of the gnat?

The far more relevant distinction, ever since 1848, is: legality — legitimacy.

Annette’s torment: the separation of knowledge and belief. That, as Lorenz von Stein recognizes, is the separation between those who possess and those who possess nothing: the former know; the latter believe.

People who are subjected to this separation without themselves carrying it through consciously—that is, people who possess no class consciousness and do not even want one—wear themselves out inside a conflict imposed upon them: unavoidable, inescapable.

What connects me with Erich Voegelin? He understood the central importance of Goethe, and understood it critically. If disaster has occurred, then from the standpoint of intellectual history it can only be traced back to the cult of Goethe. Above all, the specifically modern German idea of race can only be explained through that cult.
Everything else follows automatically once the idea spreads to the masses—once someone “dares to dare,” and the bêtes féroces, the wild beasts lurking behind every cult, are finally let loose.
With Schiller, the turn toward Goethe has already taken place (Letter 9 of On the Aesthetic Education of Man): Goethe was the perfect human being (Voegelin, p. 140).

Carus: Goethe’s “noble birth,” the supposedly innate nobility of the man of genius and the demonic man. (We shall see what comes of that at the bicentenary celebrations in 1949!) This provides the basis for racial theory: Kommerell, The Poet as Leader, 1928, on Goethe’s role as leader.
Goethe also tolerated no one beside him who refused to take part in this cult. Hölderlin, Kleist, even Schubert were all pushed aside by him.
